question: Which neural architectures learn a genuinely general rule for bilateral visual symmetry from restricted examples, rather than shortcuts tied to training-image appearance or comparison distance?

key_findings.claim: ImageNet-oriented feed-forward CNNs and a recurrent object-recognition model fit training families but fail as the uninformative center band grows.
key_findings.evidence: DenseNet, Xception, Inception, ResNet, and RCNN-SAT are trained on random-noise images with band sizes zero and four; accuracy drops by roughly 20-50 percentage points on unseen large-band families despite high training accuracy, and representation analysis points to band cues rather than a general symmetry rule.

key_findings.claim: A three-cell ConvLSTM trained from scratch is the only tested architecture that nearly perfectly generalizes across synthetic band and stripe distributions.
key_findings.evidence: Unlike a seven-layer dilated CNN and a frozen CLIP representation with logistic head, LSTM3 remains near ceiling as mirrored flanks move to image edges and reaches 97 percent on pixel-exact natural mirrored images.

key_findings.claim: Time-step and activation analyses support, but do not prove, an iterative center-out visual routine.
key_findings.evidence: More separated stripes require more recurrent steps for high accuracy, and late recurrent activation clusters emphasize the midline only for symmetric inputs, consistent with local information propagation under shared weights.

key_findings.claim: Recurrence loses its special advantage when learned from heterogeneous natural images.
key_findings.evidence: With 10,800 augmented natural crops, LSTM3, dilated CNN, and CLIP reach 88-92 percent on similar natural tests but all fail to generalize back to synthetic symmetry; lower pixel correlation predicts natural-image errors.

method.core_idea: Turn bilateral symmetry into an out-of-distribution relational-generalization assay by separating informative flanks with unseen distances and changing pixel statistics.
method.mechanism: Train architectures on only two band families, test on new band widths, stripes, and natural images, then use recurrent-step ablation, activation clustering, and representational dissimilarity matrices to infer the learned computation.
assumptions: Synthetic random-noise mirroring isolates symmetry from semantic and local-shape cues.
Generalization across band widths and stripe positions indicates acquisition of a reusable symmetry rule.
Differences among heterogeneous architectures can be attributed largely to recurrence despite unequal pretraining and optimization conditions.

techniques.role: Tests relational extrapolation as symmetric evidence moves farther apart.
Isolates comparison distance with only two informative columns.
Relates processing time to spatial separation.
Distinguishes symmetry coding from band-presence and luminance shortcuts.

evaluations.setting: Six pretrained feed-forward CNNs plus RCNN-SAT on synthetic band families
evaluations.metric: Binary accuracy on unseen band widths and luminance
evaluations.result: Networks fit seen families but lose 20-50 points on large unseen bands and encode shortcut-like band features.
evaluations.baseline: Human participants who infer the class near ceiling after few demonstrations

evaluations.setting: LSTM3, dilated CNN, and frozen CLIP on band and stripe OOD tests
evaluations.result: Only LSTM3 remains near-perfect across distances; dilated and transformer features deteriorate on edge-localized evidence.
Synthetic LSTM3 achieves 97 percent on exactly mirrored natural pixels, but all naturally trained architectures fail on synthetic distributions.

evaluations.setting: Restricted recurrent time steps and activation clustering
evaluations.metric: Accuracy by stripe distance and spatial activation maps
evaluations.result: Required steps grow with distance, while late symmetric activations concentrate at the center axis.

limitations: The strongest claim concerns 20-by-20 synthetic bilateral pixel equality, not perceptual symmetry under pose, illumination, occlusion, or three-dimensional structure.

The transformer comparison uses frozen CLIP trained on 400 million image-text pairs while LSTM3 and the dilated CNN are trained from scratch, so architecture, pretraining, input scale, and optimization are confounded.
Only one recurrent family, one principal training distribution, and limited hyperparameter search are examined; parameter and compute matching are not reported.
K-means activation maps and time-distance correlation are compatible with a visual routine but do not establish the exact algorithm or biological mechanism.
failure_modes: A recurrence advantage can disappear when backgrounds, illumination, and approximate rather than exact symmetry enter the training distribution.
Zero padding, fixed center axis, and image-size regularities may enable a center-out routine that will not transfer to arbitrary axes or transformations.
Frozen transfer representations can understate what fully trained attention or non-local architectures learn.
Binary accuracy can conceal calibration and near-symmetry sensitivity failures.
reusable_insights: Relational vision benchmarks should split by dependency distance and content family, not only random examples.
Vary available recurrent computation at test time to probe whether a model learned an iterative algorithm.
Pair OOD accuracy with explicit shortcut prototypes in representation space.
Separate exact pixel symmetry from human-perceived structural symmetry in both labels and evaluation.
open_questions: Do modern fully trained vision transformers, state-space models, or large-kernel CNNs learn the same rule under compute-matched conditions?
Can a recurrent model handle unknown reflection axes, rotation, translation, occlusion, and approximate natural symmetry in one system?
Which causal intervention on hidden states would verify the proposed center-out algorithm?
Does human neural timing scale with comparison distance in the way the LSTM predicts?

competitive_landscape.title: Do Neural Networks for Segmentation Understand Insideness?
competitive_landscape.difference: Villalobos et al. test inside/outside segmentation for arbitrary closed curves and likewise find recurrent local routines generalize; this paper applies the thesis to bilateral symmetry classification.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning long-range spatial dependencies with horizontal gated recurrent units
competitive_landscape.difference: Linsley et al. introduce horizontal gated recurrent units for contour tasks; the reviewed paper provides a symmetry-specific OOD assay and step-based routine analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Non-local Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang et al. directly aggregate all-position interactions with non-local blocks on video and image tasks; such trained non-local blocks are not included in the paper's architecture comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: Symmetry-Aware Transformer-based Mirror Detection
competitive_landscape.difference: Huang et al. explicitly engineer symmetry-aware attention and train it end-to-end on real mirror-segmentation datasets, showing that the paper's frozen-CLIP result is not a general impossibility result for transformers.

novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference: recurrent long-range visual routines and learned symmetry detectors predate this work. Its distinctive contribution is a clean cross-family symmetry assay showing that a ConvLSTM's shared iterative computation generalizes across synthetic dependency distances, alongside a useful negative result on natural-image transfer; it does not establish architectural necessity in general.
reviewer_notes: All 24 pages, both experiment sets, natural-image section, architecture/training details, analyses, and references were reviewed. Primary competitor records were checked on 2026-08-23. The title's 'inadequacy' is narrower than it sounds: it applies to the tested training regimes, especially frozen CLIP rather than a fully trained transformer.
